title: MHLA: Restoring Expressivity of Linear Attention via Token-Level Multi-Head
one_liner: Keep the cheap cost of linear attention while recovering variety in the global summary by splitting the sequence into several head-wise summaries.
lead: This linear-cost sequence-mixing method is attractive because its cost grows gently with sequence length, but it often compresses too much information into one global summary. When that happens, different parts of the sequence start looking too similar and quality drops. MHLA fixes that by letting several heads build separate summaries over different parts of the sequence. This helps because each head can preserve a different pattern instead of forcing everything through one bottleneck, while the overall cost still scales linearly.

problem.h2: Cheap sequence mixing often collapses diverse sequence information into one summary
paras: Self-attention (a method where each position compares itself with all other positions) gives high quality but becomes expensive on long sequences because the number of pairwise comparisons explodes. Linear attention (a cheaper variant that replaces the full comparison table with running summaries) avoids that explosion by updating those summaries in one pass.

The tradeoff is expressiveness. If one shared summary has to represent many different patterns at once, positions that should stay distinct begin to blur together. A vision patch about texture, a word about negation, and a video frame about motion may all compete for the same compressed summary, so the model loses the ability to keep separate global cues alive because that summary has only one mixed channel for all of them.

callout.html: Make several head-wise summaries along the sequence so the cheap method keeps more diversity, because each head can carry a different global pattern.

paras: The paper changes the summary mechanism inside linear attention. Instead of one shared sequence summary, it uses multiple head-specific summaries so the model can keep several distinct global signals alive because each head stores its own view of the sequence.

hidden.name: how many distinct global patterns survive compression
paras: The hidden quantity is summary diversity: after compression, do different positions still receive clearly different global information, or did the method flatten them into the same generic context? A model with poor summary diversity can be fast yet weak because it erased the distinctions needed for classification, language understanding, or generation.

MHLA improves summary diversity by letting each head keep its own running view of the sequence. That matters because one head can focus on one kind of long-range pattern while another head keeps a different one, so the final representation retains more variety without paying for all pairwise comparisons.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark heads that preserve distinct global cues instead of mixing them together.

reads.html: The model should keep several different long-range signals alive at once, not one washed-out average.
Word-level multi-head structure restores expressiveness because separate heads preserve different global cues inside the linear-cost attention method.

paras: Plain linear attention replaces the full interaction table with a compressed running state. That is fast, but if every position reads from the same compressed state, the model has only one channel for global sequence information. Different long-range patterns interfere with one another because they are forced into one shared memory.

MHLA widens that memory without giving up linear scaling. Each head builds its own summary over the sequence, so several global channels exist in parallel. This works because the heads can specialize: one head can preserve broad scene layout, another can preserve rare language cues, and another can preserve motion structure. The model no longer has to squeeze every long-range dependency through one narrow pipe.

The method keeps linear cost because each head still uses the cheap running-summary computation instead of rebuilding the full pairwise table. The improvement comes from better organization of the summaries, not from sneaking quadratic work back in, because the method adds parallel summaries rather than all pairwise comparisons.

math.words: For each head h, compute a separate linear-attention output from that head's sequence features, then join the head outputs. The separation is what preserves diversity.
math.equation: output(i) = concat_h ( q_h(i) * S_h ) where S_h = sum_j k_h(j) * v_h(j)
symbols: a position being accumulated into the head summary
the query for position i inside head h
the key for position j inside head h
the value for position j inside head h
the running summary stored by head h
join the head outputs into one final representation

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose there are two heads and three sequence positions.
Head 1 builds summary S_1 = 10 from cues about object layout.
Head 2 builds summary S_2 = 4 from cues about fine detail.
At position i, head 1 query weight is 0.6 and head 2 query weight is 1.5.
The final position representation uses both outputs, so it keeps two different global cues instead of one shared mixed summary.

math.note: The key change is not the running-sum form itself; it is that every head owns a different running sum.

items.b: Too few heads still bottleneck the summary.
items.html: If the number of heads is too small, distinct sequence patterns will still collide because the model has not created enough parallel summary channels.
Different heads may learn nearly the same behavior if training does not encourage useful separation, so the theoretical diversity does not fully appear in practice.

items.b: Cheap attention is still an approximation.
items.html: Some tasks may still prefer full pairwise comparison because certain dependencies need exact interactions that a compressed running summary cannot represent completely.
When heads specialize into different long-range roles, the model recovers much of full attention's strength because each head preserves a different slice of global structure.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a long-sequence classifier with three versions: full attention, plain linear attention, and MHLA. Keep the layer count and width matched. Measure sequence length, wall-clock cost, and held-out accuracy. Also inspect whether different heads respond to different long-range patterns in the input.
demo.metric_eq: gain = accuracy_MHLA - accuracy_plain_linear at matched linear-cost budget
demo.closing: The demo should show that MHLA wins when plain linear attention fails: quality rises because head-wise summaries preserve distinct global information instead of forcing the whole sequence through one shared summary.
